blocks.content: The http-basics topic mentioned that every response carries a status code, a number telling the client exactly what happened. This topic covers those codes properly, the five broad categories, and the specific individual codes that come up constantly in everyday web development and debugging.

Status codes are not arbitrary trivia, they are a genuinely useful, standardized signal, letting a client instantly understand what happened without needing to parse any actual response content at all.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784016792181-411946106.png
blocks.alt: Every HTTP response carries a three digit status code, with the first digit revealing its general category instantly

blocks.content: 1. Five Broad Categories

Every status code first digit immediately tells you its general category, even before knowing the exact specific number. 1xx codes are informational. 2xx codes mean success. 3xx codes mean redirection. 4xx codes mean a client error, something wrong with the request itself. 5xx codes mean a server error, something wrong on the server own side.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784016794143-770797381.png
blocks.alt: Five broad categories, distinguished instantly by the first digit: informational, success, redirection, client error, server error

blocks.content: {"headers":["Category","First digit","General meaning"],"rows":[["Informational","1xx","The request was received, processing continues"],["Success","2xx","The request was successfully understood and processed"],["Redirection","3xx","Further action is needed to complete the request"],["Client Error","4xx","Something is wrong with the request itself"],["Server Error","5xx","The server failed to fulfill a genuinely valid request"]]}
2. 2xx: Success

200 OK is the standard, everyday success code, the request was understood and processed correctly. 201 Created specifically indicates a new resource was successfully created, commonly returned after a successful POST. 204 No Content means the request succeeded, but there is genuinely nothing to send back in the response body.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784016795812-773084809.png
blocks.alt: 200 for standard success, 201 specifically for a newly created resource, 204 for success with nothing to return

blocks.content: 3. 3xx: Redirection

301 Moved Permanently tells the client this resource now lives at a different address for good, update any bookmarks or links accordingly. 302 Found means it is only temporarily at a different address right now. 304 Not Modified, tying directly back to caching concepts, tells the client its already cached copy is still perfectly valid, no need to download it again.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784016797409-78863392.png
blocks.alt: 301 for a permanent move, 302 for a temporary one, 304 confirming a cached copy is still valid

blocks.content: 4. 4xx: Client Error

400 Bad Request means the request itself was malformed in some way. 401 Unauthorized means the client needs to authenticate before this request can proceed. 403 Forbidden means the client is identified, but genuinely not allowed to access this specific resource regardless. 404 Not Found means the requested resource genuinely does not exist at all.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784016799061-688828991.png
blocks.alt: 400 for a malformed request, 401 for missing authentication, 403 for denied access, 404 for a resource that does not exist

blocks.title: 401 versus 403, a common point of confusion
blocks.content: 401 means, I do not know who you are, please authenticate. 403 means, I know exactly who you are, and you are still not allowed here. They sound similar but signal genuinely different problems.
5. 5xx: Server Error

500 Internal Server Error means something genuinely broke on the server itself while processing an otherwise valid request. 502 Bad Gateway means a server acting as a gateway or proxy got an invalid response from an upstream server it was relying on. 503 Service Unavailable means the server is temporarily overloaded or down for maintenance.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784016800574-827956851.png
blocks.alt: 500 for a generic server side failure, 502 for a bad response from an upstream server, 503 for temporary unavailability

blocks.content: 6. The Genuinely Useful Client Versus Server Distinction
blocks.text: 6. The Genuinely Useful Client Versus Server Distinction

blocks.content: The 4xx versus 5xx split is one of the most practically useful things about status codes. A 4xx code says something is wrong with THIS specific request, the client fault, fixable by changing what was sent. A 5xx code says something is wrong on the server own side, not something the client can fix by changing its request at all.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784016802394-411927944.png
blocks.alt: 4xx signals a client side problem fixable by changing the request; 5xx signals a server side problem the client cannot fix

blocks.title: Why blindly retrying a 4xx rarely helps
blocks.content: Since a 4xx means something is wrong with the request itself, sending the exact same broken request again will almost always just produce the exact same error again, the request itself needs to actually change first.
7. Using Status Codes for Real Debugging
blocks.text: 7. Using Status Codes for Real Debugging

blocks.content: When something goes wrong, checking the exact status code first is genuinely one of the fastest ways to narrow down where to actually start looking. A 404 means look at the URL being requested. A 401 means look at authentication. A 500 means look at the server logs, the problem is not in what the client sent at all.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784016804036-349922882.png
blocks.alt: Checking the exact status code first quickly narrows down whether to investigate the client side or the server side

8. Common Mistakes and Key Takeaways

items: Confusing 401 Unauthorized, missing authentication, with 403 Forbidden, authenticated but still not allowed, they signal genuinely different problems.
Treating every non 200 response as an equally serious failure, when a 3xx redirect is often a completely normal, expected part of an exchange, not an error at all.
The first digit alone instantly tells you the general category: success, redirection, client error, or server error.
4xx means the client should fix its request; 5xx means the problem is on the server side.
Status codes are a fast, standardized first step for narrowing down where to actually debug a problem.
